newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Single issue holds up Hebron deal, PLO says.
newsitem.headline: Single issue holds up Hebron deal, PLO says.

text.p: Haggling over further Israeli withdrawals in the West Bank kept Palestinians and Israelis from holding a summit on Thursday and sealing a deal on self-rule for Hebron, PLO officials said.
Both sides, however, continued talking despite the shooting of seven Arabs, wounded by an off-duty Israeli soldier in Hebron on Wednesday.

They said a meeting between Palestinian President Yasser Arafat and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to clear the way for a Hebron redeployment could take place any time between Thursday afternoon and in "a few more days".

"Only one issue is left and after that a summit meeting will be set," chief Palestinian negotiator Mahmoud Abbas told Reuters after eight hours of talks with Israeli Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai that ended early on Thursday.

U.S. Middle East envoy Dennis Ross was due to meet Arafat on Thursday afternoon (1600 GMT) in an effort to clinch a deal, said Nabil Abu Rdainah, an adviser to Arafat, adding: "Talks could drag on for a few more days."

Palestinian negotiator Jamil al-Tarifi said at issue was a PLO demand that Israel commit itself to target dates for further redeployments after Hebron, mostly in rural areas of the West Bank. These are redeployments already agreed in previous peace deals.

Under a 1995 Israeli-PLO peace deal, 80 percent of Hebron was due to be handed over to Palestinians nine months ago. But violence, security concerns and other issues have held it up. Some 400 armed Jewish settlers live in the heart of the town of 100,000 Arabs.

"It's almost definite that there will be some kind of summit this afternoon...and probably will be a final meeting in which the agreement will be initialled," Netanyahu's adviser David Bar-Illan said early on Thursday.
"There are no outstanding issues unless the Palestinians raise a new issue or demand the reopening of an issue that has been concluded," he said.
If initialled on Thursday, the deal could go to Israel's cabinet on Friday for approval and be signed in time for a redeployment early next week, Bar-Illan said.

The militant Islamic Jihad group meanwhile vowed in a leaflet to punish Israelis for the attack, describing the emerging deal on Hebron as "an agreement of shame" and saying the shooting would invite more atrocities against Palestinians.

The shooting, by a reserve soldier hoping to keep Hebron from getting Palestinian rule, ignited a debate in Israel over how a man some thought had emotional problems for years had been taken into the army and been issued a gun.
Noam Friedman, 22, an Orthodox Jew, emptied the clip of his M-16 automatic rifle into a crowded outdoor market, wounding seven Palestinians, before other soldiers overpowered him.

Friedman told investigators he wanted to sabotage any transfer of power in Hebron, which includes the Tomb of the Patriarchs, a site holy to Jews and Moslems where settler Baruch Goldstein massacred 29 Arabs three years ago.
The tomb is due to remain under Israeli control along with all Jewish holy places after the handover.
